utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. On Armistice Day, 11.11.11., it's Joanna Korner and Sebastiaan van Hooydonk for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, and Ms. Deirdre Montgomery, appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic and Miroslav Cuskic, appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Can -- I would like to raise a matter concerning the witness, the witness list for next week, Ms. Korner, if -- if I may. We noticed that 007 is not on the list anymore and we were wondering why that was. Is there a problem with 007, or is it only because 002 and 008 will take up the -- the entire week?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is exactly why. There are no problems at all with Witness 007, but due to the policy of the Victims and Witnesses Unit, which is the same in all cases, we put this witness on the waiting-list as a reserve, as it were. He can appear if there's a chance of him beginning to testify on Tuesday. But, in my estimate, if the trial proceeds at this pace, he may begin to testify only on Friday so that there's no chance that he may end his testimony on that day. The alternative would be that he can begin to testify and finish the examination-in-chief and then re-appear in December, but I would -- I would be reluctant to do that. Of course, everything depends on the development of the situation, but we will make sure that the witness be here in time for his testimony. However, only if it's possible to hear him at once, in one day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: But let's see, then, where we realistically go with the further cross and re-direct of 002 and 008, because, I think there is matter for discussion there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, can I say, I -- obviously yesterday and overnight I've had a look at the matters I have for this witness. I anticipate that I will do today nearly all of the areas I want to deal with him with the exception of Kotor Varos, which I would like to deal with as a discreet topic on Monday, because it is effectively the longest, but I can deal with all the other aspects of his evidence today. I anticipate, therefore, that my cross will certainly finish on Monday, and I would hope, but as I say, it's -- when I'm always saying this it's always wrong and of course it does depend to a certain extent to whether the witness can confine himself to answering my question. But, in any event, one way or the other, I will finish on Monday with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Which -- which, in reality, means the first session of Tuesday included, which we take on the Monday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: But that wouldn't -- so that -- that -- that leaves very -- very little time for -- for 008.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, as I said, we're at a moment at a loss, really, to know what it is 008 is going to cover. We accept the -- the killing of Colonel Stevilovic and the CSB guy, Markovic. And as we understand it, that's the bulk of his evidence. So I'm not at all clear what else. All we've got is he's going to talk about the Croats and Muslims in Kotor Varos. Again, we accept in Kotor Varos there was resistance from both the Croats and the Muslims. In fact, they held out until November when Vrcici [phoen] felt -- fell. And so at the moment we're not clear what evidence he's going to give that in any way we dispute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes. But we still face estimates of -- in total, procedural matters, included, four court days for 008.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't -- that cannot, under any circumstances, be right. The Stanisic Defence, as we've seen, don't have any matters to put. We were told by Mr. Cvijetic that he would take up to an hour and he took, I think, something like seven minutes in all. I don't know what their cross-examination estimate is for 008, but I -- I -- I have doubts they'll be of any length.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: In the four court days it's one hour and a half for the Stanisic Defence. So that's not the bulk of it. Mr. Krgovic, how about the chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, our estimate for the examination-in-chief is that it would certainly take more than one trial day. We had envisaged originally six hours and we'll try to make it less than five, but I always leave a margin of one hour. So it would amount to a day and a half all in all, because apart from this incident which is important for the understanding of the event in Kotor Varos, and as well as the knowledge what happened before and after the incident, and bearing in mind that these two witnesses are linked, it's very important to correlate what happened to Stevilovic and the events around the special detachment. That's why we believe it's such an important topic that we can't deal with so easily.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, and I think that perhaps, not today but at a later stage, and then we can see where it goes, I'm not at all clear how it can be relevant to call a mass of evidence about the killing of Colonel Stevilovic and Mr. Markovic, which is not the subject of any count on the indictment, nor the subject of any dispute. And it will be for counsel taking that witness, of course, to deal with it. But I merely put down, as somebody in my chambers is always saying, a marker about this aspect of the evidence. But, Your Honours, I take the view, as I expressed obviously in the e-mail which I sent when I received the Defence e-mail about the witnesses, that we've already wasted a number of days when we could have been sitting, because we haven't got the witnesses, and it is better, I would respectively suggest, that a witness is available, if there is time available. And that the highest I put it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: We'll consider what -- what has to be done 007. But one last question to you, Ms. Korner. Is there any particular reason why we should not stick to the rule that time for cross-examination is 100 percent of the time for chief?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In this case?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: In this case, I mean. In 002 --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: In 002, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, as I've explained on a number of different occasions. This is -- you can't time cross to do with chief. It gives the -- the side calling the witness the advantage, particularly of defending, to deal with it very quickly, skipping over areas which they don't like, but, which Your Honours will see I'm going to be putting to this witness. There are a number of documents relevant to this case which are on my list, not all of which I'm going to be putting either, but which the Defence just haven't dealt with but they're all relevant to the issue. And this is probably the second-most important witness that the Defence have called in their case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Could we ask the parties, both of you, and Mr. Zecevic as well, if there is a chance that we can add to the list of agreed facts the circumstances surrounding the killing of Colonel Stevilovic and Mr. Markovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Almost certainly yes, Your Honour. As far as we're concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, look, if Ms. Korner will accept, because this witness should respond why this incident is important, that Croatian and Muslim forces were very well equipped and organised, that they had over 2.000 well-armed men who were attacking Kotor Varos and that that was the reason why the conflict in Kotor Varos started, that these conflicts added fuel to inter-ethnic mistrust and that it was not, as Mr. Brown said, that Serb forces caused the conflict, all these facts, because the very fact of Stevilovic and Markovic's deaths should be viewed in the context of all these events. Their deaths are just one segment that speaks to the movements of this witness. We need to know what preceded the incident. He will be saying where he was going. His captivity in Muslim and Croat hands, and what happened after he was exchanged, so it's a perhaps -- I mean, the incident is perhaps just one half-hour in the whole of the witness's testimony, but it -- we need to know the context, just as with the witnesses who spoke about adjudicated facts. They spent very little time speaking about the fact itself but explained at length the context. I mean, the evidence of the witness about the attack is perhaps half an hour, but explaining what happened before and after will take much more time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Of course, Mr. Krgovic knows -- oh, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Could we hear Mr. Zecevic first.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I will have to join with Mr. Krgovic because I never spoke to the witness so I'm not privy to the information he is going to testify about. Therefore, I can only join with Mr. Krgovic's because I believe that his explanation is basically correct and the Defence should be given the opportunity to challenge the evidence which we heard in court from the -- from the Office of the Prosecutor witnesses. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, of course, Mr. Krgovic knows perfectly well that we're not prepared to agree to that. But that's got absolutely nothing to do with the simple fact of whether on the 6th of July, I believe it was, of 1992, the car in which Colonel Stevilovic, Mr. Markovic, and the witness were travelling was ambushed. And the two people in the car died and the witness survived. And that's the simple fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I was going to ask the, perhaps a naive question, as to whether it was impossible to separate the fact --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: -- of the killing from the why, but I think Mr. Krgovic has already answered that when -- if I'm understanding correctly what he's saying is that this would save at the most only a half-hour because the why, in terms of the context, and of course I would remind him that even with context that the matter of relevance still is -- is a criterion which would be -- which -- which would be opposed. But the -- is a half-hour worth it?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- as I say, at the moment, all of this is news to us that this is what this witness can say, and knowing what we know of his position, we're very surprised he can give the sort of evidence that Mr. Krgovic thinks he can with any knowledge. But that's, you know, all we can say. But all we can say is that we do not believe, unless it's deliberately spun out, that that witness can take five hours in-chief. And our estimate in cross-examination, based on only what we know -- and as I say all we have is a statement that he made to his own side about what happened to him during the ambush and thereafter, we have no idea how he comings by any knowledge of the other events because we've got no statement from him nor a proofing note, as I keep explaining, and that's why our estimates of cross are so difficult to give as to how all this other information is going to be adduced. But, in any event, as I say, our estimate on what we know at present is that cross-examination is not going to take more than -- that's an estimate, as I hasten to add, and I'm not going to be the lawyer cross-examining, about three hours, max.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: In addition to everything else that has been said so far, coming back to the present witness, it is our intention that he be completed with the extended session on Monday. That is, cross-examination, plus re-examination is finished so the witness is released on Monday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Well -- Your Honours, I understand. I -- I wanted to -- to add one further thing about this business of equal time for examination-in-chief and cross-examination, and that's, as I say, one of the problems you may have noticed is these witnesses answer very, very shortly the questions in-chief, and either deliberately or because they find cross-examination difficult, their answers are nothing like that in cross-examination. They run on forever and go off on a side track and that's why I say it's not really a fair proposition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, we've heard what you have said on that, Ms. Korner, and it seems that the -- what we have done up to this point and what we'll probably continue to do is that our starting point would be hour for hour, but, bearing in mind the -- what is produced in the course of the exercise, we would, of course, be open to any application for further time that any -- any reasonable application for further time that is advanced. But we appreciate the handicap under which you may be labouring.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, then, very quickly. Unfortunately, this has taken up a bit of my valuable time. What we did yesterday afternoon until quite late was we have got someone to listen and transcribe part -- parts of the interview from the actual tape in B/C/S. We've loaded them up into e-court. I am going to ask him about those specific entries. I picked the ones, I hope, fairly, which show where he could have given the answers I say that he didn't properly. We've got available, if anybody wants it, the CD of the whole interview which, of course, is questions in English, translated, answers in B/C/S, translated. And so that's what I propose to do this morning, take him through those parts. I will then ask because I think it's fair -- in fairness that the whole interview be admitted. Because I think that's -- it's really only fair to him because if I am making a bad point and the Defence want to deal with other parts of the interview, then, of course, the only way of dealing with it is if the whole interview is admitted. And if it is admitted, Your Honours, we'll say we'll MFI it -- I'm sorry, if Your Honours do admit it, we'll ask for it to be admitted MFI and we'll produce a full transcript. We just couldn't do it overnight but we can do that at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Subject to be persuaded to the contrary by the other side, that seems to be a reasonable way forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I absolutely wish that this witness, when questions are put to him, has before him all the relevant passages. If the purpose of examination by the Prosecution, as they said, was to show that he never he mentioned he was a member of that unit, he should be shown all the relevant passages where he referred to his membership, all together, not taken out of context, and that's what the witness wanted to have. And let them provide a CD over the weekend so that he can familiarise himself with all the passages that have been translated and that the Prosecution would be using. If he agrees, of course. And before that, I should like Ms. Korner to indicate to us, because of our clients, all the passages that she would be using with the witness, or perhaps these passages should be played to the witness here in the courtroom to avoid any ambush to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's why I said, in fairness. Certainly I offered and the witness deadlined. I think he said why should he spend eight hours listening to it, which is a perfectly fair point of view to take. In fact, it isn't eight hours. There are breaks and -- and all the rest of it. Your Honours, I will indicate now the passages where -- which we've had translated which will come up on the screen for the witness to read. And, as I said, I'm perfectly prepared to admit I made a mistake. I've picked out all the passages, I hope, where either he had the opportunity or when he did say, and Your Honours will see he said -- he was asked directly about this, he then, as it were, backtracked, and I hope I've picked them out. But, of course, Mr. Krgovic has the whole interview in English. He has the opportunity to re-examine on any parts that I do not use.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. I think we're clear as to where we're going. So having spent more than a third of today's first session on these preliminary matters, could we go into closed session so that the witness can be escorted back into court.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Before Ms. Korner continues her cross-examination, I remind you of your solemn declaration. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sir, yesterday we ended when we were trying to deal with the problem of your interview of which there was only an English version. We've had certain portions of it -- not translated, transcribed from the original tape and what was actually said in your language and I'm going to ask you about those parts now. You will be given the opportunity, and it's a matter for you whether you want to, to listen to the whole tape over the weekend, and I emphasise that Mr. Krgovic has the opportunity to re-examine you on any other parts that we don't deal with. So can we have up on the screen but not displayed to the public, please, Your Honour, first of all, page 16 of the transcript, which is -- that's the B/C/S. Yeah, we need the English as well. The B/C/S is 23333, 65 ter number 23333. And -- what? Both the English and the B/C/S apparently. I want in the English, please, page 16.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, did you intend to give the number 20333.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm told -- yes. 20333. That's the B/C/S has been loaded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. It's just that the transcript says 23333. Because they thought that you said 23.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, no. Sorry. Thank you, Your Honour. 20333. It should be the first -- there's only five pages in B/C/S so it should be the first. Yes, thank you very much. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, sir this is where you were asked: "Okay in 1992 are you aware that any special ... units that Stojan Zupljanin formed, to deal with the security situation that was developing in those early months, January, February, March, April? It was about the time when the check-points were being erected around the villages. Soldiers were returning from Croatia, ... causing disturbances. Are aware about Stojan Zupljanin dealing with the problem by creating any special police units or task forces?" Your reply was: "I think the dates are too early." And then the -- don't worry about the document. The next sentence. You then went on to say: "Because at the initial period there were joint or officially called mixed patrols. Two inspectors from Sarajevo. Direct connection, direct link between Banja Luka and Sarajevo still existed. I don't really know which department the two inspectors came from but they were two republican ones [sic]." Then you were asked about check-points. So we need to go to the next page, I think. Oh, no, yes. Sorry, still the same page, sorry. You were asked where the mixed check-points were, and you said you didn't know. And you then said: "Because at that time as liaison officer I was very frequently away." "Q. Are you aware if Stojan Zupljanin," I think that should be "formed," not "informed," "any special police units or task forces to deal with specific problems in the early months of 1992. Say about April of 1992 to be more specific? "I don't know whether this was April 1992, but I do know that there was a special police unit that was formed. There was a ... review, you weren't personally present --" And I'm summarising your long answer there, which you can see, I -- I think you need to go to the next -- no, no, stay on the same page -- yes, and the next page in B/C/S, I think. There is your long answer. It was: I heard you said this unit was assigned four helicopters, a number of APCs, et cetera. I know the equipment was provided by the military they insisted that the commander of that unit was supposed to come from the military ranks. Now, can I ask you, sir, why if you had nothing to be ashamed of about your membership of the special police you didn't say there and then, because you were being asked an open question, what you knew about the special police, why you didn't say you were a member of the special police?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that you have attentively read the beginning of this interview, and you will have noticed that all the questions were of a leading nature. To all questions, I provided answers according to my knowledge. This question implied that at the beginning of the year something was done. They were always trying to put things into my mouth that weren't correct, and I always had to correct what they were saying. And, here, the interpretation was actually wrong. I didn't say that the unit had four helicopters but that it was planned to have that number of helicopters. So it is important to put things in context because this is impossible. During the interview, it -- it was also said that the helicopters were never received.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Look, please, sir, just concentrate on the question. You're saying, are you, that the question, as it was phrased by Ms. Taylor, who was the investigator, "Okay, are you aware of any special police units that Stojan Zupljanin formed," was a leading question?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was leading because, even before that -- you're now focussing on only one question. Before that, another question was asked whether in January, February, March, special units had been formed, and I gave a very precise answer that it was impossible because at the time there was still contacts with Sarajevo. I personally went to Sarajevo and brought back special equipment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Don't -- I'm sorry, sir. Can I remind you we have limited time. I just want you to focus on the one question. Are you saying -- I accept entirely she got the dates wrong in the first question but then she changed it, and the question that was read to you -- said to you, and to which you gave a long answer, was: Are you aware if Stojan Zupljanin formed any special police units, et cetera, say, about April 1992. And then you gave an answer which suggested, I put -- I -- sir, that this was something entirely outside you. You had nothing to do with this.

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I didn't have anything. But could we go into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, with respect, and why -- before we do that --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sir, why should we go into private session? What is it you want to say that requires private session? You don't have to say what it is, but what's the topic?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer I'm about to give can easily serve to identify me. Very few people had anything to do with this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Going go back to where we were, sir. "Do you know who the commander of the unit was? "Its commander was Captain Lukic, whose first name I cannot remember. "Do you know of any other members or commanders, deputy commanders on that special unit? "I think it happened later that the deputy commander was Ecim. "Do you know who this unit reported to? "I suppose it was the military and the police." Why did you add the words "I suppose"? You just spent the best part of two days explaining the reporting chain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness must be enabled to read his entire answer from the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, his --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What's the problem with this kind of examination when the witness does not have the whole transcript in front of him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's there. I'm sorry, I just hadn't moved it on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Whatever Ms. Korner is asking him --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm sorry to interrupt, Mr. Krgovic. But, in fact, we can get -- that is translated. I just hadn't realised because I can't -- I think it is translated. I think it's there. It's on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I'm not sure I follow your objection, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the -- this witness's answer continues, and he goes on to explain what he said. He explains why they reported both to the military and partly to the police too.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we should let the witness read his entire answer before reading -- before answering Ms. Korner's question. Because it isn't as simple as that. One question actually contains a number of questions, and the witness then answers some of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: But we're dealing with a transcript of an interview. Is there any other practical way of dealing with it but by, as -- counsel who happens to be on her feet in this case, Ms. Korner, dealing with the passages to which she wishes to draw the witness's attention? You have the benefit of having the remainder of the transcript, and if, in your view, she has taken something out of context, as we said sometime ago, you would have the opportunity to deal with that in re-examination. I see no alternative to proceeding in that manner because the -- if I understand you were right, you would expect the witness to have before him the entirety of the transcript and before he attempts to answer any question that is put, he goes through I don't know how many pages and come back to set a context for the answer. I don't know that that's a practical way of approaching it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... I see Mr. Zecevic constantly interfering. Apart from the fact these interruptions, which are without foundation are cutting through my time, this is not Mr. Zecevic's witness, nor is it -- and for him to constantly be egging Mr. Krgovic on, Your Honour, it is quite wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I have -- Mr. Zecevic, you may take your seat. I have refrained from responding to the observations - I would use that word that you have made - on several occasions about counsel for the co-accused in the -- it seems to me that in a joint trial, which this is, it is inevitable that counsel for the co-accused would seek to assist. And unless it is something that is blatantly and totally unwarranted, it is not something with which the Bench would intervene. But could we get on with it, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, may we have a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, could you enlighten us, please, from yesterday, this witness has been challenged by you, in terms of things that, as you would have put to him, he failed to say when he had the opportunity to do it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: He's a witness. He isn't the accused who is on the stand. How much utility is there in pursuing this line of -- of -- of questions, particularly, as you have indicated, that you propose to tender the entire transcript, which, as I said yesterday, would form the foundation of such submissions that you would make at the end of the day. We are at a loss as to why so much time is being spent on these challenges.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- I tried to do that yesterday. I put my -- my challenge was simply and truthfully -- straightforward that he had not -- the trouble is, Your Honour, that the witness is -- is -- is here ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: You noticed before I -- I did pause I was considering --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Whether he should be --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: -- escorted out before we [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't have to go any further. I think it's fairly clear why I'm making the challenge. I set it up yesterday. I didn't want to go through this exercise at all. If Your Honours will recall, I, merely having put the challenge, wanted to make the interview an exhibit and for Your Honours then to decide, having read through the whole thing, and - as I say - we'll now get it fully transcribed, to see whether the challenge I was making was justified. I didn't want to do this exercise. There was an objection. That's why I did it this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So are you -- yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I understood correctly the intention of Ms. Korner, without mentioning it before the witness, Ms. Korner can go through this very quickly. She can show the witness the relevant paragraphs where he was directly asked about his membership and where he avoided answering. That's only two or three places. And his answers will clearly show what happened. Ms. Korner is deliberately avoiding this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suggested already yesterday --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is -- this is what happens. And then Mr. Krgovic puts forward the Defence theory in front of the witness who then adopts it. If there is going to be further argument, then the witness must leave court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: As we indicated yesterday, Ms. Korner, the -- your application, when it is formulated to admit the transcript, will be favourably viewed by the -- by the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So you if you make the application now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Order as prayed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Your Honours, I wouldn't have done this exercise if it hadn't been for the objections. Your Honours, what I will say is would you MFI it until such time as we get a full transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, let's me try to explain what the problem is. It was not my intention to object to the admission of this transcript through this witness, with certain reservations, of course, but this document should also be accompanied by a translation, that it should be available to the accused, and that the witness, too, should have a written version and comment on it. So if the Prosecution wants this document admitted, they should provide the translation of the transcript before the end of this witness's testimony so that he has an opportunity to review all of it. Because this way of examining, where Ms. Korner puts passages taken out of context, without allowing the witness to look at the entirety of the interview, does not really mean anything to us. We'll have had a witness who did not have a chance to look at all of the interview. We'll have evidence on -- on just separate passages.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, your point is taken about the interpretation for the benefit of the accused. But in terms of making the transcript available to the -- in terms of -- of -- of also having the entire document for the benefit of the witness, it seems to me that the flaw in that proposition is that witnesses don't volunteer evidence, they answer questions that are put. You as counsel, you have the document, and if there is anything in re-examination that you wish to put to the witness, he will be given an opportunity to answer it. But I don't know that any useful purpose will be served by him looking -- having the document and then volunteering evidence. So as Ms. Korner says, the document would be marked for identification, pending the necessary translations that have to be made so that it conforms to the rules of evidence and is admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2405, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I make it quite clear that I would be quite happy to go through all the passages and deal with them with him, but it seems to me that he has already explained, as Your Honours have pointed out, I have put my challenge, and it's a matter for Your Honours, who are the deciders of fact, to weigh up the whole interview at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, I wasn't invited to, but we should have record our objection to the proposal of Ms. Korner and the -- and the -- and the -- basically the order was already made by Your Honours. But, Your Honours, the problem is the following --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Ms. Korner, first of all, you owe me an apology for the previous --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... We would hear Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: My apologies, Ms. Korner. Could we go into closed session so that the witness could be escorted from court while we consider this --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, I'm not going to talk about the witness at all or his testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: May I, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: If I might assist you before you begin, Mr. Zecevic, the reason why we arrived at the point where we are is that, as Ms. Korner admitted yesterday, she was seeking with this whole business about the previous statement to prove the negative, that the witness, having had the opportunity to volunteer this information, didn't. And the -- that discussion began yesterday, took up quite a bit of time, and, again, you would have been present this morning as it continued. And that is why -- and she did yesterday indicate that she may have been applying to so admit the rest of the transcript because, as we said today, the -- since we're dealing with what was not said, it is -- we have the -- the -- the Chamber would see the whole transcript and would then be in a position to understand the arguments which counsel on both sides would make. Now your objection would be what? What have been what?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, thank you, Your Honours. I understand fully, and I appreciate Your Honours' position. But with all due respect, I think by this decision we are departing from the rules that we have had in this trial since the very beginning; namely, what I have -- what I feel is a problem is that the transcript of the interview of the witness who is present is admitted without the opportunity given to the witness to explain the reasons why, for example, he didn't say this or didn't say that. And I think that -- that is a departure from the previous -- previous situations that we had, because we always had -- your -- Your Honours always gave the opportunity to the witness to explain himself, and it's -- in my view, it's a correct approach because we have to be correct to the witness because there might be reasons why this -- this part was not -- this answer was not given as such or was given in this way or the other way. That is the only principle objection that I have, Your Honours. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: But short of taking two weeks to go line by line through what -- through an eight-hour transcript, is there any -- what is wrong with counsel for the -- who called him in the same way that counsel challenging the witness says that, At point A, B, X, and Y, you had an opportunity to volunteer this information, you didn't. Counsel calling him says, But at C, D, G, and H he did. I mean, is there any other practical way of dealing with it rather than, as I said, sitting here for two weeks having the witness go through line by line to say why he didn't, at these different points, say what he could have said what in counsel -- in the opposition's -- sorry, in the Prosecution's view he could have said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Again, I fully understand, I fully appreciate Your Honours, and you are right. But the problem that creates is that then the -- the -- the calling party will have -- will have to go through the -- through the whole document again, in order to establish in the re-examination that there is a reason why -- why the witness gave the answer as he did during his interview. And the only -- the only cause for all this is incorrect - incorrect - question put by the Office of the Prosecutor to the witness because the Office of the Prosecutor should put to the witness the whole -- the whole answer on a particular subject. If it does -- if it does go in four lines or four different questions, all of that should be put to the witness, not just one. And that is -- that is what is causing the problem, nothing else, Your Honours. And we would go very smoothly if we wouldn't have that situation. That is my view. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, you have something to add?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just one thing that we may have forgotten. Does the witness need to authorise his interview, sign it, and confirm that it is indeed his interview before you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner? No, I wasn't inviting a response to Mr. Cvijetic's intervention --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: No, I thought you had something to say in reply to Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I see. I'm sorry. As opposed to last. First of all, Mr. Zecevic feels I owe him an apology. I'm perfectly prepared to apologise for the fact that -- that I said on the record, from what I could see he was intervening. And as has been pointed out to me before, what happens between counsel and, indeed, on the Bench, it's perhaps not as well mentioned in court and I appreciate that and I apologise for that. Your Honours, as regards -- I see Mr. Zecevic's point to this extent, except I dispute that I'm taking it out of context. We've translated the rest of it. Where he deals with the specific descriptions it, that it's all on the translation, and I was merely pausing to ask before going on. I -- I appreciate that the accusation, maybe you're taking it out of context, which is why I was careful to put the whole thing that was said on a particular topic. But as Your Honours pointed out, it -- it would take -- it's an exercise that will take a long time and it's unnecessary because it's there to make one point. I've asked him already for an explanation. He's given the explanation. I imagine his explanation will be the same at each point, and, as Your Honours have pointed out, and I have pointed out, Mr. Krgovic has the opportunity to ask him for further explanations of what he -- why he said what he did in the interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Could we ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I was going to suggest, if we may, rather than going to closed session, that if we take a break now, slightly early, and come back in 20 minutes. Otherwise we'll have to wait while we do all this to-ing and fro-ing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: That is exactly -- you have answered the question that I was about to ask. So we would take the break now and resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We reconvene and will sit for the remainder of today under Rule 15 bis; Judge Harhoff being absent. Could we go into closed session so the witness may be escorted into court.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, one of the first documents that you were asked about when you gave your evidence in-chief was the document 2D184, which is at tab 2 of the Defence bundle. And perhaps you can be given that back by the Defence to make it easier for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, that's not the right. Maybe I've got the wrong number. I thought it was 2D184; Defence tab 2. Yeah, that's the right document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you dealt with this at pages 25413 and 25414. Because you were asked about various people on the list and their ethnicity. Now, I want to deal, first of all, with the first non-Serb that you identified, Mr. Sead Besic, who you said was a Muslim. Mr. Besic was, in fact, was he not, an ex-chief of the CSB before the multi-party elections?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And he had been, had he not --

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. [In English] I have problem with the ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This left monitor, could I switch the image so that I can see what the Prosecutor is saying?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You've got the document in front of you, sir. You don't need anything to look at the screen.

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't have the document yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You have the document I am asking you about in front of you, sir. I'm asking you about that list of names for the 17th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, could -- could you maybe explain to the witness what you mean when you say "you have before you"? Just tell him once again which document he is supposed to look at.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I can see he has got it open in front of him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, sir. You've been given -- what you're looking at on the screen on the right-hand side is exactly the same as you have in the folder before you.

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But first you said it's not the right document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Let me start this again, sir --

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. Speaking of ... I can. I can. I have looked at it. Regarding Sead Besic, his fate was the same as that of the chief of public security from Banja Luka who was a Muslim but not a member of the SDA, and he was replaced by Bajazit Jahic. In the multi-party elections many people lost their positions --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I'm -- sir, in fact he wasn't replaced. He was replaced by the chief of the CSB Stojan Zupljanin which, I agree, was as a result of the carve-up of the multi-party elections. But that's not what I'm asking you about. He was removed, was he not, from his position in Prijedor which he went to after he lost his position as head of the CSB?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know about his further career, but I know that he received this subsidy at the state security sector which means that he remained there it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: And he worked in the state security earlier, so I suppose that after the multi-party elections and the changes, he returned to his original organisation in Prijedor. And while he worked here, he travelled -- he commuted everyday from Prijedor because he was based there, and I know he was given a driver and a service car.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, no. I'm going to suggest to you, sir -- I'm going to show you that he was actually removed from his position in Prijedor in a moment but I want to stick to this document. Sir, are you suggesting to the Court that Mr. Besic was allowed to work properly throughout the whole of 1992 as a member of state security?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me something I really don't know. I was not there in the building all the time. I was in the field all the time on my own duties. Mr. Besic outranked me, and I never even had coffee about him. If you want to know about his career, Chief Kesic or some men from the top leadership of the service could tell you more.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is beyond my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's fine. Let's go on to Mr. Baric, who you told the Court was a department chief. He wasn't, in fact, was he, at that stage? After the outbreak of the conflict, no non-Serb remained as chief of a department, did they, in your organisation?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I believe he remained chief of section, just as Emir Zahirlic [phoen] at the time when these payments were made. If some changes did take place, they should be in some documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I'm going to come onto some documents in a moment. Mr. Zahirovic, again, I suggest, although he remained for a little bit longer, until 1993, he was not, as you said, chief of a line of work. Do you agree with that suggestion that I make to you?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot affirm that. I know he was a chief for a while, but was he replaced or wasn't he? I don't know. All I can see from this list is that these people were, for a time, employees of the state security and that they received payments due to them. That's all I know about --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- this period. Most of this time I spent out in the field. I really can't speak of these things.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Well, sir, we can cut this short then, because my understanding was the whole purpose of showing you this document and having it admitted into the evidence was to show that non-Serbs continued to work for the CSB effectively in the same positions as they had before and for some time. Is that -- are you -- is that what you are asserting or not? If the simple answer is you don't know and all you can say is that they were in June of 1992 on this list, then say so.

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying these people were on the list, and, as far as I know, Emir Zahirlic remained in his senior position, but I don't know how long. He may have retired at some point because he is older than I am. But I know for sure that he was chief of a line, as I know about the chief. What's his name? Milan Baric.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Let's deal with, shall we, with Nokto -- Suvad Nokto. Were you aware that on the 9th of June, so before this list was prepared because it's dated the 17th of June, together with man called Dean Brzovic, who we see next at number 27.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we go to the next page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Had both, in fact, as we'll by the document, what's called consensually terminated their employment. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What about Muharem Zjajo? I hope I'm pronouncing that correctly. He didn't stay much longer, did he, either?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muharem Zjajo --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He didn't stay much longer, did he?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Because communications were down at the time and Muharem Zjajo remained in Jajce. He was chief of the office in Jajce which was no longer under our control, so I don't know what became of him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, let's go back to the next page again, please. Well, no, see where we are. Mira Ibrahimovic, number 29. Blanko Komosar, and Mara Vignjevic. I'll give them -- I'll give the names afterwards to the shorthand writer. They were all secretaries, were they not, as was Nisveta Dervisic?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were not secretaries.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You told us that Nisveta Dervisic was --

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment. Nisveta Dervisic was but that's the problem with the Prosecution. They constantly try to put in my mouth something additional that I didn't say. It just detracts from your credibility. I only said that Nisveta Dervisic was a secretary, whereas Mrs. Blanka and -- could you repeat the third name? Who else did you mention? I can't find it here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If you look at numbers 29, 30, and 31.

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mara Vignjevic and Blanka Komosar and Mira Ibrahimbegovic did certain specific jobs in operations technology. They were not secretaries.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And what were those specific jobs?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I know for a fact -- sorry. Are we in open session?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, we are. No, we're not going into private. If you want to add -- all right. You want to go into private session, do you? Do you want to go into private session?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Private session, if Your Honours agree. I'm sorry, I say all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As you know, I prefer the whole thing to be in open in any event.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: (redacted).

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And, in fact, you said that you thought Mira Ibrahimbegovic was from a mixed marriage. She was, in fact, a Serb, was she not, married to a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I was looking at the last name and thinking that she might have been from a mixed marriage. That's what usually happened in mixed marriages. One child would be given a Serb name; another child a Muslim name. I just said it because of her surname. I really don't know her CV, so I can't say anything for certain. I just said it was possible she was from a mixed marriage because of her name, although she could have been a pure Muslim, too, because there are Muslims with that first name, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Let's just have a look, then, from the documents as you say you don't know one way or the other what actually happened to some of these people.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we have a look, please, at... sorry. Yes, it's P805, tab 46A. Deal, first of all, with Mr. Besic. This is a report which I'm not suggesting you would have seen before. Well, you may have, I don't know. Because it's an SNB report, dated 20th January 1993. It's a report on the work of the Prijedor SNB. And then, in the paragraph that we can see, second paragraph, "The Prijedor SNB had 12 employees at the beginning because of combat operations in the Prijedor area ... four members of the section," and do you see Sead Besic were removed from the list of persons with war-time assignments. He was removed because he was a Muslim, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He was removed because he moved to Banja Luka, as far as I know. I think he spent the entire war in Banja Luka from what I know, but I think it's verifiable in the section that deals with transfers.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Let's move onto the next name.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we have a look, please, now at a document which is 20324, at tab 39. No, that's not it. 20324. It's the book. Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is -- the letter doesn't matter so much. It's 22nd of September, from Stojan Zupljanin to the bank about salaries. At the same time, we hereby inform you that of the 18 of our employees on the list, seven have left this service. And if we look at this list, next page, please, in English and B/C/S. The seven who have gone, there we see Mr. Brzovic, and Mr. Josip Ladan, who was number 24 on the list of names that you looked at. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now let's look, please, at document, which is -- oh, sorry. An error there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Can we look at document number ... 03102.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before that, may I say something about this list?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's Mustafa Maglic [phoen], among others, on the list, a Muslim from the area of Travnik or Vlasic. I know that he left the service because, when he was out in the field, in that village - what's its name? - Turbe he had been beaten up by his own countrymen, Muslims, because he was a native of that area. And he left the service after that. He was beaten up when he was going out into the field or returning from the field. And Stipe Djukic, he left the service because he found a job in Austria and emigrated. Not all of them were laid-off. And this write-off of interest was done for everyone who made an application.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no, [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If somebody applied for it, the chief would right for this paper for them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Sir, you know perfectly well the point I'm making. Just a minute, sir. We didn't need your story about -- just a moment, sir, then you can finish. All I am asking you about is that the names you identified on the list that you were shown by Mr. Krgovic. Now it may be very interesting to hear about a Muslim who was beaten up by other Muslims, but I just want to deal with those people who are on your list. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only wanted to let you know that the list is not necessarily true. That somebody is on the list does not mean that they were removed. There may be other reasons at that time. We did not receive our salaries regularly and that's why this problem occurred. Some people who had difficulty making ends meet, people who lived in town and had no village relatives to help them out had to look for a different job, and there was a time when we didn't receive our wages for six months.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sir, you know that you made a gross error when you said to Mr. Krgovic what you said and gave the impression that all these people continued to work in the CSB?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I object. The Prosecutor should tell us where I asked that question and where the witness made that answer. I showed him the list and asked him how many people continued in their jobs. And he did mention some people, but he didn't mention any of the names that the Prosecutor asked him about, and he didn't say they continued in their jobs. I would appreciate it if the Prosecutor would stop misleading the Court and misrepresenting the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is just time-wasting. Each and every one of the names that I have gone through may be found mentioned by the witness at pages - what did I say? - 25415. I have specifically limited myself to those names.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm just asking for a transcript reference where I told -- put it to the witness that all these remained in their jobs all the time. If you can provide me such a reference, that be would fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, that's two -- again, Mr. Krgovic, he accuses me of asking two things rolled up into one. This is bluff and bluster. I am continuing to answer -- to ask these questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, can we look, please, at the document, as you won't accept that that letter shows, for example, that Mr. Brzovic was no longer working by September. Can we have a look, please, at the document that the number I mentioned earlier, which was 3 -- 03102. Thank you. Now, before we go any further, do you recognise this book? Because, in fact, sir, your name appears in it.

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I cannot remember this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: By the way, are we back in -- are we in open or private session? Open. Thank you. I want to just deal with two entries, then, please. The first is -- in the English, it's at page 19. In the B/C/S, I'm not sure what page it is in B/C/S. Oh, sorry. English is page 9 in e-court - thank you - and the B/C/S is -- no, sorry. Page 29 in e-court, and 19 in English. 29, B/C/S; 19, English. Do you see there the names Suvad Nokto and Dean Brzovic consensual termination of employment? There's an error, I think, in the date because if you go on it says -- it appears to say the 19th June but it's actually obviously the 9th.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We need to go -- sorry, we haven't got -- could you go, sorry, down to the in B/C/S I'm not sure -- no, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here, I can only see, although you don't like to hear that, that Sead Besic got some sort of certificate.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you look, please. I appreciate --

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, that's coming up now, down there. Consensual termination of employment, Dean Brzovic. I know that began to -- that he actually opened a private business involving electrical appliances. I don't know about Suvad Nokto.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, could we have P1373 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is Mr. Kesic submitting a payment, the June list, in fact, the one we looked at earlier, for the SNB, and do we see there that Mr. Ladan has been removed from the salary list? Mr. Ladan, who was 24 on the original list. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And, finally, on this one, the last document, the August payroll, please, which is 65 ter number 20335, at tab 37A. This is the submission of the August 1992 payroll. And do we see there that Muharem Zjajo and Nisveta Dervis, respectively numbers 25 and 36 on the June list, are removed?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At that time, I think that there were no more communications with Jajce and that the State Security Department had already been separated. Muharem Zjajo was chief of the detached unit, as far as I know. We had no contacts anymore because Jajce was already separated from the municipalities that joined -- I'm not sure what it was called at the time, the AR Krajina or something.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I agree. I accept entirely that there was fighting, although Jajce fell eventually. But that doesn't effect, does it, Ms. Nisveta Dervis?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dervis? Well, we had one Nisveta Dervisic. But I don't know this one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, this is one of the people that you identified on the list of people --

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The list reads Nisveta Dervisic. And here, I see Nisveta Dervis. Dervis is a man's first name, and I believe that it originally means the member of a religious order in the Muslim religion.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you know, honestly, we don't need that sort of remark. It's clearly, isn't it, an error in spelling. That's all.

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe you can enlarge it. I can't make it out here. Or if you have the original that you can show me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Have a look -- okay. We'll enlarge that part in B/C/S, please. It's in line --

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just enlarge it. Let me just see. Ah, this reads Dervisi. Dervisi sounds like Albanian. But it may be a typographical error.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a fact, though, that we had no jurisdiction over Jajce at the time, so it was normal to adopt such a decision. I really don't know about Nisveta when this happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And, in fact, if we went through the whole list, that we haven't got time to do, we'd see that all the people I'd mentioned no longer appear on that list.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I ask that this list be marked and admitted? This payroll, rather.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an objection for reasons of principle. This is a totally new exhibit that doesn't live up to the criteria from the instructions issued by the Trial Chamber for leading evidence. Ms. Korner chose one way of examining the witness. Instead of asking him the way I did which of these people worked and which he saw after a certain date, and this could have been done very easily, and now we heard the answer of this witness, and, to my mind, there's no need to tender these documents. If it's about the credibility of the witness, he, at no time, said that Ladan and Zjajo are -- remained on the job after the cut-off date.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Of course, the disadvantage that we have is that we only have the cover and not the list.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, it carries on. I don't want to waste time going through it. But you -- you'll see that none of the people I've just gone through with him figure on this payroll in August. Your Honour, I'm dealing with what could only be, otherwise there was no point in taking this witness through it. The implied assertion was, look, effectively, the CSB wasn't prejudiced against non-Serbs or whatever. They just went on working, and what we're doing is dealing with that assertion. And this is one document out of the many I've put to him. I've not sought to admit the others, but this is the one document that shows that all the people with whom I dealt and with whom he dealt in his evidence in-chief on the list no longer appear on the payroll by August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2407, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, let's move, please, to the special police. Now, let me see if I understand your evidence, and I'm going to break it up, the general tenor of your evidence? The bulk of the special police was made up not of police officers or reserve police officers but military personnel. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Are you saying that there was only one platoon that contained police officers and the rest all contained military personnel?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it was mostly that way. There was one police platoon, then there may have been some personnel changes, but in principle there were three platoons of soldiers and one platoon, even less than that, of police. I only know that one of the commander's names was Tuskasic [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Are you saying that there was -- the platoons were kept completely separate? In other words, those made up of military personnel all served with other military personnel in a platoon, and those made up of police officers all served in separate platoons? In other words, there were not mixed personnel within the platoons. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know that they were all billeted at Rakovacke Bare; that is, in one place. And I think that the police platoon mostly comprised police officers. And the other platoons, at least as far as I know, because after 20 years I cannot be fully concern, but as far as I know, in the remaining three platoons there were only soldiers, military personnel, and the commanders of the platoons were also military personnel.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Answer my question: Is it your assertion that the platoons were not mixed; in other words, ex or military personnel together with police? Are you saying that there was a complete separation?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were together. All four platoons belonged to the same unit. They were billeted together, and I forgot to say that food was also provided by the military. There was a field kitchen, and we got a certain quantity of food. And we had food cards for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, forget --

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no, stop.

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's possible. But in principle we only manned one platoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think it's a mistranslation. It's not what I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But he also -- he was also answering your question when you interrupted him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, but that's not the question I'm asking. That's only -- I think there's been a mistranslation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What I'm asking you is not whether you all ate together or all stayed together or what you did, but whether the personnel assigned to the platoons were mixed in each platoon. In other words, each platoon had some police officers or reserve, and some military.

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. I was told that one of the platoons was a police platoon and that it was attached. And that they were looking for people belonging to SJBs to man that platoon. Now how that went, but the -- one of the commanders was a police officer and probably the platoon was also manned by police officers. That seems logical to me. But it can be verified against the list, and it can be established who was a police officer and who wasn't. Possibly --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- they were also members of other platoons. But one of them was a police platoon. It was called that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Stop, please. I mean, you know, sir, if you're doing this deliberately so that we don't get all the questions in, then please stop. I told you twice now: Just answer the question I ask. It does not need a long explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the problem is that Ms. Korner is interrupting the witness. The witness had begun to answer her question when I intervened. The police platoon didn't have enough personnel and there were also soldiers. That was --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was the beginning of his answer and she interrupted him, and that's the problem. You should let the man finish his answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The question I asked was a simple one and I'll continue. It is not, therefore, your case, it is not what you assert, is it, sir --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: By the way, are we in open session? Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Are you saying -- you're not say, rather, that there were two types of special unit. One which was -- no, don't bother about the documents. We're coming onto the documents later. Just listen to the question, please. You are not asserting there were two types of special unit; one which was police and one which was military?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. You are not suggesting, sir, are you, that one part of the special police was reporting through the police chain of command and another part of the special unit was reporting through the military chain of command?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When a unit is headed by a military officer, they all report to the military officer. The unit commander, if he's a soldier, certainly, he -- certainly there's a relationship of subordination with regard to the military leadership. I mean, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Let's not -- I tell you what, let's not, for the moment, just deal with the principle. As you say, and I accept, there is a command structure. The member of the platoon will report to his superior officer; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: His superior officer, the head of the platoon, will report, in turn, to his superior. The head of the unit, or the deputy head, if he's not there?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: To Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. And if Mr. Lukic wasn't there, to whom would the head of a platoon report?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: To his deputy.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And let's say, for example, unavoidably, both the head of the unit, Captain Lukic, and Mr. Ecim, who was next in line, they were not there, to whom would the head of the platoon report?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: To whoever was on duty. Somebody had to be on duty at any given time, and then they would report to him. That's normal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It is inconceivable, sir, isn't it, that the police, whether the minister or Stojan Zupljanin, would have agreed to pay people who were military carrying out military function as policemen in those circumstances?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where the problem is, if that's -- if that was a decision of the political leadership as it was, it had to be obeyed. It was not up to us. Allocations were made in the budget and they were used for it. The money could not just be sucked out of thin air. It's a large sum of money. I paid out salaries myself, so I know that a decision had to back that up along with a fund for special purposes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. No, no, no -- yes.

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can see that from --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You've made your point. And what I'm putting to you is that you're actually not telling the truth about this, sir. Do you understand that? This is nonsense what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think your claim is nonsense, if I may say so. You don't understand our financial system and our financial transactions. Because if, at a certain level a decision is made to pay 100.000 or a million Deutschemark, that money has to be paid to that beneficiary, not a different one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry, sir --

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's logical, and please don't take offence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry, sir. Again, I am afraid it's -- What I'm suggesting to you is: What you're saying about the special police, in fact, not being police at all but military and not even reporting through the police chain of command, is untrue. That's the suggestion I'm making.

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I affirm that I've told you the truth, that effectively and factually that unit was controlled by the army. And you could see that from the very activities of that unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Now, sir, what you're saying -- it also follows logically from what you're saying that members of the military become policemen only to be resubordinated back to the military. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's precisely how it was. Because that unit was set up and automatically resubordinated because the man number one in the unit was a military man, and all its activities were identified by the military intelligence officer, and we only received an information about it only inasmuch as we asked for some funding or equipment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's just nonsense, isn't it, sir. Absolute nonsense. That -- that somebody goes to the -- the -- the -- the -- the ... I'm trying to find the right word. Just let me finish and then you can answer. To say that somebody would bother to get members who were under military control to, on the face of it, become policemen and then give them back to the military. It's complete nonsense, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't agree with you. It's not nonsense. It was the political decision then. For certain structures to be established as police units; whereas, in effect, they were sent to accomplish typically military assignments. And you can see that clearly from their activities. Anyone who knows anything about military tactics and operation will understand that. Now why somebody decided to call it a special police unit, I don't know. People plan and envisage things in many ways that do not come out as they thought. It was originally planned for the unit to have helicopters as well, but we never got them. And we were never really a police unit. We were -- we were fed by the military.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
